subject.spine: David, Lusia, Shimon and Dov. Every other thread returns to these four.
but_it_is_not_only_them: THE WIDER FAMILY AND ITS HISTORY. The paternal line is documented back six generations to Abraham Abe Rapaport, born 1784 at Tarnów, whose gravestone survives. Galicia, the timber and tannery trades, the rabbinical connections, and how a Jewish family of that region lived — and how many of its children did not reach two years old.

THE RESEARCH ITSELF, as a second narrative. This archive was built in three months of 2026 by a family and two researchers, and the discoveries are dated events in their own right. That thread has a shape: a wrong town on a document, a passport application that cracked a dead end, a chart that named a great-great-grandfather, a living cousin who had been looking for us.
THE OBJECTS THEMSELVES. Show the documents and the photographs on screen. They are catalogued here with their readings, their evidence levels and their file paths.
subject.note: Everyone else in the archive is material standing behind the four — but "standing behind" does not mean invisible. The research thread is what lets an audience feel how nearly all of this was lost.

discoveries.title: Family Tree research begins
discoveries.description: Magda connects Dalia, Dana, Doron and Daniel with Basia (Polish genealogist) over WhatsApp. The 'Family tree' group is created. The goal: trace David, Leah, and Shimon Rapaport's journey for Dov's 80th birthday in August.

discoveries.title: Brussels DP card identified
discoveries.description: Basia finds a DIPIS Displaced Persons card for David Rapaport, born 25.12.1911, registered in B. on 9.04.1946, headed for Palestine or USA. The date of birth matches exactly. The card lists Cieszyn/Tesin as birthplace and parents Bernard and Regina née Grunfeld — which conflicts with family information.

discoveries.title: BREAKTHROUGH: David's birth record found in Nadwórna
discoveries.description: Ms. Kasia at the Jewish Historical Institute (ŻIH) in Warsaw finds David's birth certificate in Nadwórna. Confirms: parents Berisz Rapaport and Rebeka Griffel, daughter of Leizor Griffel and Sara née Chajes — merchants of Nadwórna. ALSO finds Rebeka's own birth certificate (1888 Nadwórna). The 'Cieszyn' on the DP card was a transcription error. Two new generations and the verified birthplace — all on one day.

discoveries.title: 🗺️ Every Virtual Trip card now shows the address in Google Street View
discoveries.description: All 13 Virtual Trip cards now embed two side-by-side iframes: the OpenStreetMap location plus a Google Street View pegman view at the exact coordinates — labelled 'How it looks today'. No API key required. Click any card to see the place AS IT LOOKS RIGHT NOW.

discoveries.title: 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 Attribution updated — Dalia, Dana, Doron and Daniel as equal partners
discoveries.description: All attribution language throughout the archive (events, people, places, documents, hypotheses, research center, multilingual UI strings) has been updated to credit Dalia (mother), Dana, Doron and Daniel Rapaport as equal partners in this birthday gift to Dov. Mother and three children — one family voice.

discoveries.title: 🏕️ Cyprus camp numbers DOCUMENTED — Karaolos 55/60/61/62/63 (summer tents) vs Dekhelia (winter huts)
discoveries.description: British internment camps in Cyprus were organised in two clusters: SUMMER tent camps numbered 55, 60, 61, 62, 63 at Caraolos/Karaolos north of Famagusta, and WINTER Nissen-hut camps at Dekhelia/Decauville near Larnaca (~50 km away). 53,510 Jews detained 1946-1949; ~2,200 children born in captivity. David's family was held ~8 months. JDC Archives only holds the Aug 1948 - Feb 1949 birth lists — for the family's roster look at Yad Vashem and USHMM databases.

discoveries.title: 🚢 The Theodor Herzl ship VERIFIED — ex-HMS "Guardian", Newcastle 1907 (NOT Exodus 1947)
discoveries.description: The Aliyah Bet ship that carried David, Lusia, Shimon and infant Dov from Sète to Cyprus on 2 April 1947 was the ex-British cable-laying ship HMS/SS "Guardian" — built 1907 by Swan Hunter & Wigham Richardson in Newcastle, 1,768 tons, triple-expansion engine. Acquired by Mossad LeAliyah Bet in 1946 and refitted at Marseille. Distinct from the SS Exodus 1947 (ex-President Warfield), with which it is routinely conflated.

discoveries.title: 🏠 Lusia's wartime apartment building IDENTIFIED — Prospekt Svobody 24, Lviv
discoveries.description: ulica Legionów 24 in 1942-1944 Lwów is today's Prospekt Svobody 24, Lviv: a four-storey Biedermeier stone kamienica built 1836-1837 by architect Johann Salzmann for F. Adamski. Polish national poet Wincenty Pol lived there 1856-1866. Lusia rented an upper-floor apartment as 'Maria Cizlik' while a German military base fired guns from across the central promenade. Current photo of the actual building now embedded in the Virtual Trip card.

discoveries.title: Berisz’s 1924 passport application names his parents
discoveries.description: The paternal line had been a dead end even for Edward Gelles after twenty-five years. Basia found the passport file, and with it Moses Saul Rapaport and Menukha — and a photograph in which Dana saw a resemblance to her father.

discoveries.title: Three Tarnów marriage deeds independently name the apical couple
discoveries.description: Read from the scans by Claude vision: the 1919, 1920 and 1923 marriages of three of Berisz’s sisters, each naming "Moses and Menucha" as their parents.

discoveries.title: A living cousin on the paternal side — and she wants to meet Dov
discoveries.description: Yehudit Shlomit, daughter of Zwi Ayalon Nussbaum and named after Freida, Berisz’s sister. She worked at Yad Vashem and had been looking for our branch for years — she once tried to reach Dov through a school essay Dana wrote at twelve. Dana spoke with her for an hour.

discoveries.title: Jente survived — the 1941 list of Jews in Liège
discoveries.description: Her daughter Szewa appears on the 1941 census at 5 Place Delcour, and the 1946 Liège marriage record states that the bride’s mother, Jenta Rapaport, was living together with her daughter. A great-grand-aunt whose fate had been blank.

discoveries.title: Szabse Rapaport, rabbi of Dąbrowa Tarnowska
discoveries.description: Basia, from the Tarnów notarial records: "they convinced me that Szabse was your ancestor." He served until 20 April 1884 — and it explains at last why Berisz’s passport registers the family commune as Dąbrowa, a town nobody could account for. The same evening, from a different direction entirely, Dana produced a record naming Schabse with Figa/Yete.

paragraphs.text: For a year this family could go back no further than a name on a passport. The paternal line stopped at Berisz Rapaport, and even Edward Gelles, who spent twenty-five years on the Rapaport rabbinical genealogies, could not carry it past him. In May 2026 Basia found the passport file itself, and inside it were his parents: Moses Saul Rapaport and Menukha.

Berisz was born on 30 July 1886 in Radomyśl Wielki, and the family's registered commune was Dąbrowa Tarnowska — a town nobody could account for until July 2026, when Basia read the Tarnów notarial records and found Szabse Rapaport serving as rabbi of Dąbrowa until 20 April 1884. That is why the passport says Dąbrowa. The same evening, from a completely different direction, Dana was sent a record naming Schabse with Figa/Yete.

Three marriage deeds from Tarnów — 1919, 1920 and 1923, for three of Berisz's sisters — each independently name the same couple as their parents. Three separate clerks, in three different years, writing the same two names. That is as close to certainty as this kind of research reaches.

David Mendel Rapaport — Memek — was born in Nadwórna on 25 December 1911, son of Berisz Rapaport and Rebeka Griffel. Nadwórna sat in the Carpathian foothills of eastern Galicia, then Austria-Hungary, then Poland, today Nadvirna in Ukraine.

His Brussels Displaced Persons card of 1946 gives his birthplace as "Cieszyn (Tesin)" — a town four hundred kilometres away, where no one in this family ever lived. It is a transcription error by a French clerk, and it is worth pausing on: here the document is wrong and the family's memory is right. That is why nothing in this archive ranks paper above testimony as a rule.

Leah Weitzner — Lusia — was born in Bolechów on 8 April, daughter of Elias (Eliyahu) Weitzner and Matel (Matylda) née Weinreb. Every record agrees on the day. They do not agree on the year: the Bolechów civil register says 1913, while her own survivor card, the ŻIH index and the Haifa burial register all say 1916. Three against two, but the two include the civil register. It remains unresolved.

In 1933 her parents left for Mandatory Palestine. Lusia stayed. It is a small sentence with the whole of what follows inside it: she would not see them again for fifteen years, and the war would fall on the side of the family that remained.
sources: Memoir ch.1 — family testimony, no document held

paragraphs.text: They married on 10 February 1935 in Bolechów, her own town. She was twenty-one and he was twenty-three.

Her memoir puts the wedding in Muszyna, in February 1938 — three years later and in another town. Written forty years afterwards, the memory placed the marriage at the opening of the Muszyna years rather than three years before them. The month is right in both. And the record resolves something the memoir left broken: under her date, Shimon arrives eight months before his parents marry; under the register, he is born two and a half years into the marriage.
Shimon was born on 22 June 1937 in Lwów. The family had long said "Mosina" — a name that turned out to be Muszyna — but his own survivor card, filled in after the war, says Lwów.

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. What the family did over the next five years is known almost entirely from Lusia's testimony, because almost no one who could have written it down survived to do so.

She tells of Przemyśl under Soviet administration; of the Nadwórna ghetto and David's escape from it hidden in a wooden wagon; of false identities in Lwów; of the Hormak family, and of neighbours named Pietrozycki and Ivanov who helped them; and of Shimon, three years old, kept in a crate for two and a half years so that he would not be seen or heard. No document we hold corroborates any of it. That is not a weakness in the account — it is what happens when the people who would have kept the records are the people who were killed.
sources: Memoir chs.3-6 — no corroborating record held

paragraphs.text: Two things from those years are on paper. David was stripped of Polish citizenship in 1942. And his father Berisz was murdered at Auschwitz — our research associates him with victim number 188161, a reading we have asked the Arolsen Archives to confirm or correct. No Page of Testimony was ever filed at Yad Vashem for Berisz or for Rebeka. This archive is, at present, their only written memorial anywhere.
sources: Yad Vashem name search, 21 May 2026 — nil result

narrative.title: Katowice — and a separation nobody recorded

paragraphs.text: The war ended and they came west with the repatriation, to Katowice. On 1 July 1946 Lusia and Shimon each filed a survivor-registration card at the Katowice committee — cards 151738 and 151337, mother and son, one after the other.
sources: CKŻP cards nr 151738 and nr 151337, Katowice, 1 July 1946

paragraphs.text: But David had been registered as a Displaced Person in Brussels since 9 April 1946 — three months earlier. On the day he was recorded in Belgium, his wife and son were still in Poland. He had gone ahead, and they followed later that year. The memoir says only that "the family reaches Brussels and stays in a hotel": one movement, everyone together. The two cards, held in this archive since May and never read against each other until August 2026, say otherwise. It is the first of the two separations in this story.

David's Displaced Persons card describes a forestry engineer, Polish nationality stripped in 1942, speaking Polish, Italian, German, Czech and Russian. It is the only document that reaches across from the war into what came after.

Dov Bernard Rapaport was born in Brussels on 28 August 1946. No Belgian birth registration is held in this archive — it is the easiest missing document of all, and only he can request it, as the person the record belongs to.

On 2 April 1947 David and Shimon sailed from Sète in southern France aboard the Theodor Herzl — the ex-British cable-layer HMS Guardian, built at Newcastle in 1907, carrying 2,641 ma'apilim gathered from camps across France and Belgium. Shimon was nine. Lusia stayed behind in Brussels with the seven-month-old Dov.
sources: Palyam / ship histories — the vessel is fully documented

paragraphs.text: On 13 April the Royal Navy boarded her off the coast. The passengers fought; three were killed and twenty-seven wounded. Everyone aboard was deported to Cyprus, and David and Shimon were interned at Karaolos, north of Famagusta, for about eight months. The camps there held 53,510 Jews behind wire between 1946 and 1949, and some two thousand children were born inside them. Shimon was released from Atlit in 1948.

Lusia sailed from Brussels with Dov on the Kadima. She had waited more than a year alone with the baby, working, while David and Shimon were behind wire. The Haifa burial register records her year of immigration as 1948 and David's as 1946 — the two-year gap the memoir describes, written into their own graves. Dov's first journey was with his mother, the two of them.

In Haifa she saw her parents for the first time since 1933. The family settled on Abbas Street, and later bought an apartment on Moriah Street with German reparations — money David argued with himself about taking. He worked as a customs broker, the trade his son Dov followed, and then his grandson Doron.

In 1986 a granddaughter, Hadas, asked her teacher Esther Weiss for help with a school assignment, and Esther sat down and interviewed Lusia. Ninety pages in Hebrew. Without them, almost nothing in this archive between 1939 and 1948 would have a voice at all.

David died on 29 August 1990 and Lusia on 28 December 1996. They are buried beside one another at Sde Yehoshua, graves 102ד and 102ג. Her burial record names her father Eliyahu and her mother Matilda — the same two people her memoir opens with, sixty years earlier and in another language. The last page of the record matches the first page of the testimony.

events.title: The Theodor Herzl is boarded by the Royal Navy

Three ma’apilim were killed by gunfire and their names are known: AHARON DOV, PINCHAS WEISS and MENACHEM SAMET. The wounded and the sick were taken to the Atlit detention camp; everyone else was deported to Cyprus. David and nine-year-old Shimon were aboard.

events.description: Read from the ketubah itself on 2 August 2026: "here, in the holy community of Haifa, may it be rebuilt speedily in our days" — the place is written into the document. A machine reading in June 2026 had given Brussels and flagged an oddity, that the document said "on Shabbat" while the date fell on a Friday. documents.title: Descendant chart of Abraham Abe Rapaport — Basia, 2026
documents.archive_reading:
THE CHART THAT NAMED MOSES SAUL’S PARENTS. Read 5 August 2026. It descends from Abraham Abe Rapaport and carries document thumbnails above most cards, so Basia is working from registers rather than from other people’s trees.

The card that matters: SZABSE RAPAPORT, born 30 January 1823 at Tarnów, died 1884, married to ITA FEIGA JAHR (died before 1897). On the sibling bar beneath them sits MOSES SAUL RAPAPORT, born about 1858, died 8 November 1933 at Tarnów, married to MENYCHA LEINER.

Every particular matches what this archive already held independently — the Tarnów death record 1933/152 gives the same death date, the same age and the same two parents, and we had Menukha’s maiden name Leiner from the Sambor marriage record of 1913, which Basia did not use. The chart adds two things we never had: Ita Feiga’s maiden name, and Szabse’s date of birth.

Also on that sibling bar, so also children of Szabse and Ita Feiga: LIEBE (b. 28 March 1847), MAJER (b. about 1849, d. 22 October 1920, married Cerka/Cecylia Margulies) and IZCHAK CHAIM (d. 15 August 1921, Kraków). Moses Saul had brothers and sisters, and this archive did not know their names an hour earlier.

The chart reaches further back still — Herschl Rapaport, born about 1792 at Tarnów, died 23 May 1874 — and outward across Tarnów and Kraków. It has NOT yet been read line by line.

documents.title: The Lurie Legacy — Descendants of the Shach, with Basia’s 2026 overlay
documents.archive_reading:
Basia’s marks run our line up into a published rabbinical genealogy. Highlighted in pink and named on the sheet: MOSES SAUL, and IZCHAK MAJER CHAIM — the same brothers who stand beside Moses Saul on her own descendant chart. Above them she highlights SHABTAI, A.B.D. Dombrowa, died 1897, with an arrow to the Weidenfeld sheet; and higher still ABRAHAM ABALE, A.B.D. Tarnow, died 1872, the head of her chart. The ascent continues through Isaac Rappaport, A.B.D. Pinczow (1741-1774), to SHABTAI HaKOHEN — the SHaCH, 1621-1662 — and across to Saul WAHL and Israel KATZENELLENBOGEN.

HOW THIS ARCHIVE TREATS IT. The documented line stops at Szabse and Ita Feiga. Everything above them is a published compilation, and the Davidic descent at the top is TRADITION — held exactly as the Rapaport-Kohen priestly lineage is held: recorded, attributed, and never stated as proven descent. It is kept deliberately apart from the part we can put a record behind, so the documented part cannot be weakened by association if the traditional part is ever challenged.

NOTE THE CONFLICT: Rosenstein’s Shabtai died 1897, Basia’s own chart has Szabse dying 1884. See h_szabse_death_year.

documents.title: Application for Palestinian Citizenship — Hirsch Herman Nussbaum and Inge née Rosenbusch, Haifa 1945 (31 pages)
documents.archive_reading:
Read page by page on 3 August 2026. It is a Government of Palestine, Department of Migration file: APPLICATION FOR PALESTINIAN CITIZENSHIP, headquarters serial 90563, held by the Israel State Archives (גנזך המדינה) in the Mandate Government series מ, file 3211/050.

APPLICANT: NUSSBAUM, Hirsch Herman. Wife: Inge, maiden name Rosenbusch.

What the file states:
  • Applicant's Polish passport no. 118839, issued at PRZEMYŚL on 21 September 1938
  • Wife's German passport no. 94, issued at BORKEN on 10 July 1935
  • First entry into Palestine: 12 October 1938; immigrant registration HA/5934/B of the same date
  • Wife and children registered HA/4302/A on 22 August 1938
  • Marriage solemnised at HAIFA on 12 June 1941 — Haifa Jewish Community Rabbinical Office certificate H-49343 of 15 June 1941
  • A son, MORDECHAI YOSEF, born at Haifa on 25 April 1943 — certificate 1591/43 of 14 May 1943
  • Fee of 250 mils, receipt 715052 of 29 October 1945; application made at Haifa
  • Approved 29 November 1945; naturalisation certificate no. 48628
  • Both passports withdrawn at Haifa in 1946

WHY IT MATTERS, AND WHAT IS NOT YET PROVEN. Our tree holds Zwi (Hirsch) Nussbaum, born in Przemyśl in 1919 — father of Yehudit Shlomit Ayalon, the living cousin found in June 2026, who is named after Freida, Berisz's sister. Zwi is Hirsch. A Polish passport issued at Przemyśl in September 1938 fits a nineteen-year-old from that town leaving for Palestine, and he entered three weeks later.

That is a strong lead and it is NOT a proof. The pages read so far carry no birth date and no parents' names for the applicant, which are what would settle it. The wife here is Inge Rosenbusch and the recorded child is a son, Mordechai Yosef; we do not know the name of Yehudit Shlomit's mother. Nussbaum is not a rare name. He is therefore NOT attached to any person in the tree until the particulars page is read.

NEXT: the remaining pages of the file almost certainly carry the applicant's declaration with date and place of birth and his father's name. Reading those decides it either way.

documents.title: Zygmunt Griffel — Przegląd Drzewny press feature, 1938 ('Export sets to Palestine')
documents.archive_reading: Article 'Eksport kompletów do Palestyny' (Export of sets to Palestine) listing Galician-Polish timber firms exporting to the British Mandate. Identifies 'Zygmunt Griffel Lwów (Segal, Żupnik, i Wilf)' — confirming the Muszyna sawmill operating under the holding-name 'Segal-Żupnik-Wilf' (per Żebrowski's Holocaust article) was Zygmunt Griffel's company. This is the key citation that linked Lusia's Muszyna hotel to a Griffel-family timber operation.
documents.held_at: Przegląd Drzewny (Polish Timber Review), 1938 issue. Found and cited by Basia 21 May 2026.

documents.title: Zygmunt Griffel — Sejm Album industrial feature, 1934/35
documents.archive_reading: Zygmunt Griffel was David Memek's first cousin once removed — son of Dawid Mendel Griffel Sr. (Rebeka's brother, Leizor Griffel's eldest son). This page establishes him as a major Galician-Jewish timber industrialist in 1934-35: 60,000 t/year to England, a five-port operation, with ambitions to brand Polish softwood. The 1938 Muszyna sawmill operating under 'Segal-Żupnik-Wilf' (per Rafał Żebrowski's Holocaust article) is identified in 1938 Przegląd Drzewny as a Zygmunt Griffel front company. Lusia's Muszyna hotel Willa Helin was in Zygmunt's sawmill town — the family-business ecosystem extended from Lwów-Gdynia exports down to Carpathian spa-town milling.
